strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: multivariate forecasting under channel-specific sampling periods, inter-channel dependencies, and block-wise test-time missingness.
The proposed architecture is well aligned with the stated setting, using channel tokens, masked attention, dynamic patching, and patch masking to avoid naive interpolation.

The empirical section is reasonably broad within the authors' benchmark suite, covering several modified public datasets, one industrial dataset, multiple standard forecasting baselines, ablations, and error bars.
The appendices add useful implementation details, missingness studies, masking-strategy ablations, and spectral analyses that help explain the intended motivation.
weaknesses: The main evaluation does not compare against the most relevant class of prior work: irregular/asynchronous time-series forecasting and missing-aware models. Regular forecasting baselines are mostly forced through interpolation or zero filling, so the central advantage is partly built into the experimental setup.

The benchmark construction is largely synthetic and heuristic: public datasets are manually resampled according to assumed channel frequencies, and the block-missing setup is closely aligned with the proposed patch-masking mechanism. This limits confidence that the gains generalize to naturally asynchronous data.

The novelty is moderate. Channel tokens, read-only/masked attention, patch dropout-style training, and FFT-based patching are plausible components but mostly recombinations of known ideas, with limited theoretical or empirical justification for why this particular design is necessary.

Fairness is not fully convincing: CTF uses masks and sampling-period structure while baselines are not comparably adapted with time encodings, missingness indicators, imputation-aware variants, or architecture-matched controls that receive the same metadata.

The reported gains are often modest, especially in the asynchronous-only setting, and the conventional benchmark results are not clearly state of the art. This weakens the claim of a broadly superior forecasting framework.

Scalability and efficiency are acknowledged as concerns but not quantified. Full attention over local and channel tokens may be expensive for high-dimensional sensor systems, yet no runtime, memory, parameter, or channel-count scaling study is provided.

Some method details are underspecified or internally confusing, including the definition of a 'strong dominant frequency' for FFT patching and apparent inconsistencies between the main attention-mask description and the appendix masking descriptions.

Reproducibility is limited by the lack of clearly stated code release, unclear availability of the CHS dataset, and incomplete details on hyperparameter selection and baseline adaptation for the proposed practical setting.

The central evaluation setting is mostly constructed by manually downsampling standard synchronous datasets and injecting synthetic missing blocks. This weakens the claim that the method is validated under genuinely real-world asynchrony and missingness.

The missingness evaluation favors the proposed patch-level masking design, especially when missing blocks align with patch lengths. It is unclear how robust the method is to arbitrary missing patterns, partial-patch missingness, or realistic sensor failure distributions.
